The Flydubai co-pilot accused of stabbing Capt. Smit Machchhar and trying to crash a Dubai–Tel Aviv flight has been identified by U.S., Israeli and Arab media as Hamam al-Hammami, a 29-year-old Omani national.

His name is spelled Hamam Al Hammami in some reports, because Arabic-to-English transliteration produces a new spelling for every database it meets.

While training at Oman Air in 2024, al-Hammami was allegedly found with extremist material and assessed as a security risk.

The airline reportedly removed him from flying duties but allowed him to continue in an administrative job. His now-deleted LinkedIn profile listed almost seven years at Oman Air, then Royal Air Maroc from June 2025 to January 2026, followed by roughly eight months at Flydubai.

CNN reports that his LinkedIn account published two posts about nine hours after the attack.

One video included cockpit footage of a Boeing 737 Max, zoomed in on an El Al aircraft at Dubai International Airport and ended with images of former al-Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahiri and Humam al-Balawi, the al-Qaeda-linked suicide bomber who killed seven CIA personnel and two contractors in 2009.

CNN could not verify who uploaded the posts or whether they had been scheduled before the attack.

Other accounts say he was born in the UAE to an Omani father and a Syrian mother, spent considerable time outside Oman, including in Syria, and had been influenced by extremist ideas there.

These details come from unnamed sources quoted in media reports. They are leads in an investigation, not an official finding on motive or organizational links.

Oman reportedly barred him from the cockpit over extremism concerns. Royal Air Maroc employed him. Flydubai put him on a Tel Aviv route.

In the aviation industry, this passes for cross-border mobility.

Bentonite Hills, USA

Just east of Capitol Reef National Park lies one of Utah’s most surreal landscapes—the Bentonite Hills. Born from volcanic ash over 150 million years ago, these undulating mounds look less like Earth and more like another planet entirely.

Swirling bands of red, purple, gray, and blue ripple across the terrain, painted by ancient minerals and eons of geological change. There are no marked trails, no crowds—just open silence, vast space, and a scene so otherworldly it’s been used by the Mars Desert Research Station for astronaut training.

The surface is fragile and easily scarred—best appreciated from a distance or a mindful vantage point. 🪐
